paraphrase: When the soul, put to sleep by beginningless māyā, awakens, it knows the unborn, sleepless, dreamless, non-dual (Lord) — glossed (quoting the Prakāśikā): when the soul, put to sleep by Viṣṇu's will, the beginningless māyā, is awakened by that same will, it sees Viṣṇu.
speaker: Madhva
notes: The verse is Gauḍapāda-kārikā 1.16 in the Advaita numbering; Madhva reads it as śruti. checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions

paraphrase: On 'prapañco yadi vidyeta ... māyāmātram idaṃ dvaitam advaitaṃ paramārthataḥ': 'advaita' is the supreme Brahman, known as it truly is; 'dvaita' is what is known otherwise, wrongly, by the ignorant; 'māyāmātra' means made by his will (māyā = icchā); 'paramārthataḥ' means from the Supreme Lord. The 'prapañca' that ceases is the soul's relation of owner to body; this wrong knowledge, produced by his will, ceases by his will when Brahman is known.
speaker: Madhva
notes: Gauḍapāda-kārikā 1.17 in the Advaita numbering; Madhva's text places it in the Upaniṣad (khaṇḍa 2, v. 9). checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions

paraphrase: The Supreme Self, present in the bodies of all beings, is fourfold — Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña and Turīya — and all these forms are full of bliss and knowledge. Hari as Taijasa, abiding in the mind, makes the dream appear; as Prājña he is lord of deep sleep, in which the soul, having reached Hari and covered by darkness (tamas), neither desires nor sees; Viśva presides over waking.
speaker: Madhva
notes: Mantras 3–7 of the Upaniṣad. checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions

paraphrase: (Quoting the Brahmāṇḍa:) Viṣṇu in his Turīya form abides at the dvādaśānta; it is the form attained by the liberated and is not seen in ordinary life; to those fully concentrated who have reached the sixteenth kalā and have direct vision, the Turīya state is sometimes seen. The Turīya gives all knowledge to the liberated and is the cause of all their activity; he stills the world of bodily bondage, and so is called 'prapañcopaśama' and 'advaita' (without equal).
speaker: Madhva

paraphrase: Homage to Viṣṇu, whose nature is full bliss, knowledge and power, the fourfold enjoyer of all. In this Upaniṣad Varuṇa, in the form of a frog (maṇḍūka), praises the fourfold Nārāyaṇa (quoting the Pādma); the syllable Om designates Hari, in whom all is woven, the full one, the same in past, present and future.
speaker: Madhva
